milestone: Alfr3d Deck is live on Google Play
description: The Android home screen is now a download away: free core, with a $6 one-time Pro unlock through Google Play Billing -- no subscription. Getting here meant standing up a proper company developer account, clearing Google's review of the sensitive permissions, and rebuilding the built-in file explorer on Android's own folder picker so the app no longer needs blanket access to every file on the phone.

Full JWT Auth + RBAC shipped across all 5 phases: backend login/refresh/logout, a permission matrix on all 56 write routes, webapp + Deck sign-in, rate limiting, no username enumeration, self-service/admin password reset -- tagged v0.2.0.
Every integration credential (Home Assistant, SmartThings, Spotify, ESPHome) is now Fernet-encrypted at rest, with a zero-downtime dual-read fallback for existing plaintext rows.
ESPHome added as a new local-only IoT provider, alongside a device-registry-backed multi-camera streaming model.
Household user management landed end to end: self-service profile editing, full owner/admin CRUD and password-reset, and first-run onboarding for new installs.

A durable household event log replaced a 20-item RAM buffer; a card feedback loop lets situational-awareness cards learn when a household ignores them; a shared per-cycle context frame cut redundant DB reads by about a third.
Learned baselines widened from single appliances to per-resident departure times and a household-level "is today unusual" check.

A 12-item situational-awareness roadmap deployed to production in one pass -- event log, card feedback, calendar conferencing, structured cards, anomaly detection, self-hosted routing, plus 3 items investigated and correctly stopped on real evidence.
Leave-by travel guidance rebuilt on a self-hosted OSRM routing engine plus the free Nominatim geocoding API -- no Google API key, no per-trip cloud call.
A Nexus quick-controls panel shipped: up to 10 favorited smarthome devices as toggle/dial tiles, opened from the Nexus Core.
Repos migrated to the Littl3-1-Engineering GitHub org, and the Kit's hardware base switched from a Raspberry Pi 5 to an N100 mini PC, restoring margin after a CAD-verified cost check.
Free spatial launcher with a $5.99 one-time Pro unlock live since v0.1.28 -- CI builds a debug APK on every push, with a signed-release workflow on version tags.
Custom Colors theming shipped as a 5th Pro feature: user-defined accent colors via an in-app HSV picker.
Added a rotation-lock setting and required sign-in (Keystore-backed credentials) for write actions -- device control, resident edits, running or editing a routine.
Gained the leave-by travel-guidance display, backed by the new self-hosted routing engine.
Repo migrated to the Littl3-1-Engineering GitHub org.

milestone: Situational awareness cards: August 2026 in review
description: Household composition awareness: a card reading who's home versus away, and known versus unknown devices, surfaced on the Ambient Brief with urgency-aware styling.

Cross-surface continuity: a new backend endpoint plus routines and now-playing tracking, so the launcher can offer to pick up where you left off -- resuming music paused elsewhere, or a routine edited on the web dashboard.
Rhythm-break anomalies: learns each device's typical on/off rhythm from history and flags anything still on well past its usual pattern, such as a light left on much later than normal.
Attention telemetry: the launcher reports rolling attention and dwell telemetry to a new backend endpoint, feeding the focus and wind-down signals.
All four were built and unit-tested on both sides, but none was verified on-device, and the rhythm-break baselines had no real data accumulated yet.
Site launched at littl31.com: index.html (pitch), alfr3d.html (product + pricing), lab.html (R&D showcase).

alfr3d.html got real descriptive copy for the Launcher, Core, Cloud, and Kit cards, plus a fix for a scroll-reveal crash that had been silently blocking content sitewide; a splash-logo animation crash on the homepage was also fixed.

Pricing strategy evolved across the month: from the original Core/Launcher/Cloud plan, to a Kit-first ladder ($399 Founding-100 / $449 steady-state plus a Butler subscription), to a simplified 3-SKU lineup -- then a CAD-verified parts-cost check found the Kit underwater on margin, prompting a hardware pivot from a Raspberry Pi 5 to a cheaper N100 mini PC.
Repos migrated to the Littl3-1-Engineering GitHub org.

Pricing strategy evolved across the month: Cloud and Cloud+ were retired as tier names, folded into a new Relay + Butler ladder, then simplified further by folding Relay into Butler. A CAD-verified cost check on the Kit (which bundles free Relay for life) prompted a hardware pivot from a Raspberry Pi 5 to a cheaper N100 mini PC to protect margin. The corrected Canadian-dollar parts costs and a revised market-growth range (12-20%) also reset the first-year Kit sales estimate to 40-100 units.
Earliest known concept/build in the Alfr3d lineage.
Early 2014 iteration of the home-automation daemon.
2014 iteration, ordering relative to MK-I/MK-II unconfirmed.
Home-automation daemon running on a Pi (/home/alfr3d/alfr3ddaemon.py), audio handling.
Added Python LIFX integration (pylifx).
Server + mobile companion apps split out: Alfr3dServer, Alfr3d4Android-Original, Alfr3d-MKIII-Android, alfr3d.io.
Separate repo from the 2015 MK-IV Notion page, not yet reconciled with it.
Repo explicitly describes itself as "Successor to Project Alfr3d" -- a rebrand attempt that didn't end up replacing it. Active Feb 2018 to Oct 2020 (239 commits, confirmed via GitHub commit history).

First Kafka message-bus architecture (topics speak/environment/device/user) -- direct architectural precursor to today's Kafka-based backend. Active Sep 2022 through May 2026 (434 commits) -- notably overlapping with the start of the current consolidated rewrite rather than a clean handoff.

Build one Kit end-to-end and time assembly before publishing the $400 Founding-100 price. Validates the current ~$235 CAD parts-cost estimate (N100 mini PC, NVMe SSD, PSU, enclosure, cooling, cabling, packaging) plus assembly labor, shipping, fees, and a support/DOA reserve against a real build, not just parts pricing.

milestone: littl31.com commerce: Stripe Checkout + Founding 100 preorder
description: Top GTM priority: give the Kit and Uplink pricing tiers a real visitor-to-customer path -- every rendered CTA is still a mailto: waitlist link. Backend checkout wiring staged 2026-09-09: create-checkout-session now sells only catalogued products (kit-founding, kit-steady, uplink-annual, uplink-monthly) through a server-side product-key -> STRIPE_PRICE_* map in functions/_shared/catalog.js, never a caller-supplied price ID, so test-to-live is an env-var change. Each of those four tiers in content.yml carries a dormant checkout block that no template reads yet. Still gated, nothing charges a card: no Stripe Prices or secrets set, no checkout frontend, no subscriber storage (webhook.js cases remain stubs pending the Uplink relay identity store). Remaining: create the Stripe Prices (multi-currency), set the Pages secrets, build the checkout frontend + success/cancel states, wire the webhook to subscriber storage, update pricing copy + privacy policy section 2.
Pre-commit checks, secret scanning, dependency updates, linting and CI are now in place on all three repos. Only Aikido security scanning remains, blocked on a paid plan.

Generic device control now has a SmartThings path alongside Home Assistant, but nobody in the household owns a SmartThings device, so it has never run against real hardware. Parked until one shows up.
Personality panel currently shows call-count usage only; per-token usage metadata from the LLM client isn't surfaced yet. Minor — a future-enhancement aside, not a scoped plan.
Push notifications to the launcher; depends on Alfr3d Uplink Phase 3 shipping first.
Have the launcher push on-device now-playing (any media session, not just Spotify) to the backend instead of only backend-side polling. Documented as a deferred fast-follow, not yet scoped.
Its own todo/ folder was checked directly and contains only a completed bugfix note (mobile scramble jitter fix); no forward-looking roadmap items exist for the site itself.
Abstract audio-source interface so playback isn't Spotify-only — local library, Tidal, YouTube Music, radio — plus a loose future-ideas list (NLU voice control, Last.fm scrobbling, multi-room sync).

Attribute calendar/Gmail integrations to individual household members instead of one shared global account. The login and permissions groundwork is in place, so this is parked by choice rather than blocked: two household-privacy questions still need a decision first, whether members see each other's calendars by default and whether another member's mail can be announced aloud in a shared room.
Three parked options beyond the already-shipped HLS pipeline: WebRTC for sub-500ms latency, recorded/archived playback, and computer-vision motion/person detection.

Remote-access relay (no port forwarding) + push notifications; "thin, dumb-pipe relay" that never sees plaintext data. Now scoped into a phased plan in todo_cloud_relay.md: architecture spike -> subscriber/billing identity + Stripe -> relay/tunnel -> FCM push -> security review. Deliberately a separate identity system from household RBAC auth. Not yet built.

Physical enclosure for the ALFR3D device + peripherals (mic/speaker/camera/sensors), matching the dark tactical/glassmorphic visual identity. Not currently scheduled — blocked on the hardware phase starting and a finalized bill of materials.

milestone: Kit ordering / Uplink signup commerce plan
description: Phased plan to give the Kit and Uplink pricing sections a real path from visitor to paying customer — site currently has zero CTA/checkout links on either tier. Phase A: free waitlist/interest-capture forms. Phase B (gated on Kit waitlist signal): Stripe Checkout for the one-time Kit purchase. Phase C (gated on the Uplink relay being built): Stripe Checkout + Customer Portal + magic-link login alongside the relay's own subscriber identity. Planning only, not started.

milestone: Explore: Alfr3d Deck as a new context source for situational awareness
description: Explore feeding the launcher's own on-device signals (attention/dwell, foreground app, etc.) back into the backend's situational-awareness engine as a new context source, alongside existing presence/device signals. One candidate signal, BLE presence sensing, was investigated directly and set aside (see "BLE presence sensing -- explored and set aside" above) -- modern phones rotate their Bluetooth address, so nothing personally-carried stayed identifiable in a real scan. The rest of the signal list (WiFi leave/arrive, named context zones, car Bluetooth, etc.) remains unexplored.

milestone: Clean up GitHub CI/CD, security & Aikido CVEs (all repos)
description: CI is live and the site's CSP, clickjacking and GitHub Actions hardening shipped in September. What is left is triaging vulnerabilities from Aikido scanning, blocked on a paid plan.

milestone: BLE presence sensing -- explored and set aside
description: The household's hardware can scan for BLE devices just fine, but real scans found no personal device (phone, watch) with a stable enough identity to track -- modern phones deliberately rotate their Bluetooth address. Only fixed smart-home gear (TVs, a smart light) stayed identifiable, which isn't useful as a presence signal. Re-checked again a few weeks later, just in case -- same result, same devices, same verdict. Set aside unless a wearable with a genuinely stable address enters the household.

A planned next step for the household event log -- noticing that one event usually follows another, and gently flagging it when it doesn't -- needs real weeks of history to learn from honestly. The event log itself is brand new, so this is queued rather than built against too little data.
The compact one-window settings mode on the launcher is getting a proper design pass in Figma before more building: narrow screens, every theme and accessibility sizes. Not started.

milestone: ALFR3D's own settings, reachable from the phone launcher
description: Household settings that live in the web interface today will also be reachable from the launcher's Settings, respecting each person's role. Designed, not started.

milestone: Cleaner look and animation for device controls
description: Smart-home device controls are getting a visual refresh: smoother, quieter animations and a cyan-only palette, with magenta kept strictly for faults. Not started.

milestone: One theme across the web interface and the phone launcher: web and backend
description: Pick a theme once and it follows your account. The web interface now saves your theme and applies it on every browser you sign in to, and picks up changes made on your phone straight away. Live on the household's server.

milestone: Event log times in your own timezone
description: The scrolling activity log over the wallpaper, the status screen and the built-in terminal now show event times in your phone's own timezone instead of UTC, and keep up if you travel. The web interface got the same treatment, and the backend stopped sending a few malformed timestamps that made some entries hard to read. Deployed and checked on a real phone.

milestone: Alfr3d is learning what's normal for each person and the house
description: After a weekday spent out when nobody was expected to be, Alfr3d couldn't tell it was unusual. Situational awareness now sits on a learning foundation: two years of household history is cleaned and shaped into data Alfr3d learns from, producing learned routines for who is home when, room climate, activity and the household's typical day, each with a confidence score. Drift detection notices when a routine genuinely changes. One shared engine combines those signals into judgments like 'someone is away unusually', 'a day off nobody planned' and 'an unusual day for the household', and it checks the calendar: a booked event explains an absence, while an empty calendar makes a day at home more surprising. Checking the new judgments against the old rules turned up real flaws, so they were reworked: whether someone has stayed unusually long is now judged against that person's own past stays, and a day off against their own past days, so a part-time resident's ordinary day at home no longer looks suspicious. Rule by rule, the old fixed-threshold checks are being switched over to what Alfr3d has learned; the rest keep running quietly beside the existing rules until their comparison shows they agree.

milestone: One theme across the web interface and the phone launcher: launcher side
description: The launcher follows your account's theme for Deep Cyan, Tactical Amber and Light, with a Settings switch to turn it off; wallpaper and custom-colour themes stay on the phone. Verified on a real phone in both directions and released in Alfr3d Deck 1.0.3.

Alfr3d Deck gets a full visual redesign without changing what it does. Pick Halo & Whisper, Tactical HUD or Quiet Butler as your home screen; Quiet Butler leads with the most important thing right now, whether that is an urgent alert from Alfr3d or the next event. Radial menu wedges now fit the screen edges in any orientation, and the built-in terminal has been retired.

milestone: Samurai Wisdom: a daily quote in the corner
description: A quiet corner of both the phone launcher and the web interface shows a daily samurai quote in vertical kanji, with its reading and meaning, styled to your theme. It can be switched off in Settings.

milestone: Alfr3d speaks on your phone when nobody's home
description: With spoken notifications turned on, Alfr3d now speaks through your phone when the house is empty, even with the screen locked, and stays silent if no phone is listening. When you are home it keeps speaking from the house as before.

milestone: Compact Settings: the whole page in one window
description: An optional one-window Settings layout with no tabs, built from the launcher's glowing HUD rings, with a 50-design ring catalog to choose from. A Figma redesign pass is still ahead.

Alfr3d finally learned to tell time: one shared clock, built from the household's own wake, sleep, sunrise and sunset routines, replaced six that disagreed, so it no longer says "Good morning" at 10pm. Its personality quirks became occasional instead of constant, and two more dashboard themes (Matrix and Graphite) arrived.

The "leave by now" travel card fired for real in an actual household for the first time, after calendars started refreshing every fifteen minutes and event times began reading in the household's own timezone. Leave-by cards also stopped being capped at a 30-minute heads-up.
Two years of situational-awareness history is now kept (up from 90 to 180 days), with disk growth tracked over time.

ESPHome met its first real sensor. Live temperature and humidity now flow into the dashboard; the first real device exposed two bugs, a network scan that would have found nothing on a real home network and a control panel that would have crashed on the sensor's data, both fixed before anyone hit them.

Room comfort alerts: Alfr3d says so when a room gets too warm, cold, humid or dry, then learned what is normal for each hour and recalibrated its thresholds against real household data. Along the way it found that its learned baseline could never fire and fixed that, and that power-cycling the sensor orphans its history (a mitigation is in, the root cause is still open).
An old leftover integration that forwarded the household's live activity feed to a public notification service was found and removed the same day.

The system-health panel stopped crying wolf: container health now comes from each service's own self-test (13 of 13 report a real verdict, up from 5) instead of being inferred from CPU load, and three services that had silently dropped off the panel are back.

Resilience fixes: services that consume messages now restart themselves after a power outage instead of waiting for a manual restart; a cache bug that silently dropped every payload containing a decimal number is fixed; power control works again for media players such as a Samsung TV; and welcome announcements no longer "correct" the wrong name.
The first real live "unusual departure" alert was found in production history, which confirmed the rhythm-break detector works on real data.

Self-service updates (v0.4.9): Alfr3d detects a newer version, an authorised household member applies it with one click after re-entering their password, a database backup is taken first, and it rolls itself back if the new version doesn't come up healthy.

milestone: Situational awareness across Backend and Deck: September 2026 in review
description: Alfr3d can be told what to call you (a first name, "boss", "Dr. Athos"), set per person from the web or the launcher, and "sir" and "madam" are banned outright.

The launcher now checks in with Alfr3d about every half hour in the background, only with enough battery and politely backing off on bad networks, so cards are current the moment you pick up the phone. A Background Sync switch is in Settings.

With explicit opt-in, Alfr3d can learn your movements away from home. It is off by default, approximate only, goes only to your own server, is read only while you use your phone, and stops and clears the queue when switched off.

The brain and the launcher stopped guessing separately: each fact (time of day and routines, battery and do-not-disturb) is now owned by whichever side actually knows it, and each falls back to its own estimate if the other can't be reached.
Alfr3d notices when a guest has quietly become part of the household: a guest's influence on the mood fades the longer they stay, and after about two weeks it suggests promoting them to a resident.

Every loading spinner and plain circular button outline across the web dashboard and the Deck's Socket radial menu became a family of animated HUD rings, each shape carrying a fixed meaning and honouring reduced motion. Design recreated from Goran Spasojevic's animated HUD buttons, credited in both apps.
Renamed from "Spatial Launcher" to Alfr3d Nexus Launcher and then to Alfr3d Deck, with Socket as its radial menu. "Nexus" now belongs to the web dashboard alone.
Socket was reorganised so common destinations sit one level shallower, with nothing more than three steps deep.
Alfr3d Shell grew from a toy into a real command line in five phases (device and app management, filesystem, live Alfr3d control, window management). It was later retired in Deck 1.1.
First-launch setup was rebuilt as a five-step walkthrough; long-pressing any app opens a real context menu; the app list survives being killed in the background.

A real crash was found and fixed: reinstalling or restoring the launcher onto a new phone could crash it on every launch because Android's backup restored sign-in data whose key does not survive. It now recovers on its own.
Play Store prep: targeting Android 16, code shrinking verified on a device, a privacy-policy gap closed, the listing rewritten, and device deletion added to the Devices window.
The site leads with what Alfr3d is, "the only home butler you own", instead of a category label; every feature claim was checked against what the engine really does in production.
Every ".99" price was rounded to a whole number: Deck Pro $6, Kit Founding-100 $400, Kit Steady-state $450, Uplink $10/month or $100/year. The pricing switcher also gained real CAD/USD/EUR rotation.

A Content-Security-Policy and an anti-framing header went live (the latter at the Cloudflare layer, since GitHub Pages can't set headers), alongside tighter build-pipeline permissions and a scrubbed repository history.

milestone: Deciding what is free and what is Pro in Alfr3d Deck
description: A review of exactly what sits behind the $6 Pro unlock, checking that the app and the pricing copy promise the same thing, and deciding where the new features (Compact Settings, Samurai Wisdom, theme sync) belong. Core usability stays free. Not started.

An opt-in second tier on top of today's approximate location. Android's approximate setting is only accurate to about 2 km, which makes everything near home look like one place, so Alfr3d can't see a local walk or tell "home" from "nearby". Stays off by default and sent only to your own server. Not started.
Settings to choose a transparent or solid status bar, and light or dark icons and text. Not started.

Camera stream addresses include the camera account's login. They will move into Alfr3d's encrypted secrets store like every other integration credential, decrypted only when a stream starts, with existing cameras migrated in place. Not started.
A locale-aware currency toggle (CAD, USD, EUR) with an easter egg: hover and the price scrambles into "Alfr3d Scrip". This item is the symbol design; the toggle and scramble are a separate build.

milestone: Open in Maps from calendar events
description: When an event has an address, the launcher will offer both Open in Maps (in your default maps app) and Open in Calendar, instead of guessing which you meant.

milestone: Transactional email for Uplink and orders
description: Platform news, order confirmations and shipping confirmations sent from Alfr3d Uplink and commerce infrastructure. Household Kit units themselves never send email, and email codes for first-run setup were rejected because claiming a unit already requires being on its network. Not started.
A speculative look at whether a physical dial can control Alfr3d through a local API or Zigbee2MQTT, with no cloud dependency. Nothing is committed until that check is done.

On the Tactical HUD home, panels now do something when you tap them: the situation report opens your brief and the household panel opens the residents list, next to the daily samurai wisdom card. Compact Settings now lets you switch home style and visual effects from the one-page layout, and the radial menu no longer gets blocked by open windows.

milestone: Alfr3d Deck 1.2.0: secure pairing that survives a new IP address
description: Your Alfr3d now makes its own private certificate authority at home, and keeps its HTTPS certificate current whenever its network address changes. The Deck pairs with that authority once, after you confirm its fingerprint, so a new IP address or router no longer breaks the connection. If the authority ever changes, the Deck warns you instead of trusting it. Works with local certificates only, no public certificate authority needed. Existing installs pair once more. Ships in Deck 1.2.0.

milestone: Alfr3d's old fixed rules start giving way to what it has learned
description: Three of the old fixed-threshold rules now run on what Alfr3d has learned about this household. The indoor-climate notice compares a reading with that hour's usual instead of one wide daytime band, so ordinary afternoon warmth no longer sets it off. The 'deep in it' focus notice judges window switching against the household's own hours instead of a fixed count of fifteen. And the household's 'unusual day' now chooses its own yardsticks -- device activity, time spent at home and how busy each kind of event is -- and sets its own bar from the household's past days, aiming for roughly one notice every two weeks rather than a hand-picked bar that had never once been reached. Comparing old and new side by side also turned up and fixed a check that had been silently failing every minute, and the comparison now measures how often a learned rule would speak, not how closely it copies an old rule that was often silent. Indoor temperature and humidity are now shown to the nearest degree and percent.
